fixes.explanation: The high priest asks Stephen, “Are these charges true?” No small talk, no warm-up, just a question you could answer with one word. Hold onto that, because Stephen has a whole lot more than one word coming. The question was about the charges, and that's all it was.

That's a fair question to ask somebody, but it isn't the one in the text. The high priest asks Stephen, “Are these charges true?” He's pointing right back at what the false witnesses just said. Nobody in this verse asks Stephen for his credentials.

Abraham is right, friend. Stephen says, “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran…” Abraham is the man Stephen calls “our father.” Starting here is like opening a family reunion speech with the great-great-grandparents.

Noah, who built the ark (Genesis 6:22), is a good name, but Stephen doesn't use it here. He says the God of glory appeared to “…our father Abraham…” Stephen is also placing him in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran. Noah never comes up in this speech.

Descendants is right. Stephen says God promised to give possession of the land “…to Abraham and his descendants…” So the promise reaches past Abraham to the people who would come after him. Meanwhile, Abraham himself has no inheritance there, not even a foot of ground.

That's it, friend. God says the descendants “…will come forth and worship Me in this place.” Back in verse 4, Stephen said God brought Abraham “…into this land where you are now living.” So the worship is promised for the very land the council is standing in.

That's a sneaky one, but no. Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans (Acts 7:4), but that isn't where God says they will worship. God says they “…will come forth and worship Me in this place.” That place is the land God brought Abraham into.

Jealousy is right. Stephen says, “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt.” The twelve patriarchs come from Jacob, and the ones jealous of Joseph are his brothers. And Stephen adds right away, “But God was with him…”

The text says nothing like that. Stephen gives the reason himself: “Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt.” That's the brothers' own jealousy. Stephen doesn't mention their father in the sale.

Punish isn't the word. Stephen says Moses assumed they would understand that God was using him “…to deliver them…” His people were the ones being mistreated, so this was about rescuing them. God did say He would punish the nation that enslaves them (Acts 7:7), but that's not what Moses assumes here.

Not quite. The text says Moses assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him “…to deliver them, but they did not.” Nobody in the verse is giving a test. It's about rescuing the people who were being mistreated.

Midian is right. Stephen says, “At this remark, Moses fled to the land of Midian, where he lived as a foreigner and had two sons.” That remark had two parts: who made Moses ruler and judge, and whether he wanted to kill the man like he killed the Egyptian. That's a long way to travel because of a comment.

Obey is right. Stephen says, “…our fathers refused to obey him. Instead, they rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.” Moses received living words to pass on, and the fathers refused to obey him. That's a big gap between what they were given and what they did.
